summary: Shim6 is a mechanism for site multihoming in IPv6, letting hosts keep connections working when a site has several providers. This informational RFC discusses considerations on where Shim6 and its support protocols apply.

eli5.summary: If your house has two roads, a shim helps you switch roads without the mail getting lost. This memo talks about when that trick makes sense.

questions: what is ipv6 multihoming with shim6
how does shim6 handle address changes
what are the security implications of shim6
subtitle: When and how to use IPv6 multihoming with the Shim6 protocol.

tldr.problem: IPv6 site multihoming using the IPv4 approach (multiple provider-independent prefixes) would cause routing table bloat. IPv6 needs a different solution that lets sites stay connected to multiple providers without using global routing resources.
tldr.mechanism: Shim6 runs on each host and creates a layer-3 shim that makes re-homing events transparent to the transport layer. When one path fails, the shim finds alternative address pairs and continues the connection using a new source and destination address pair (locator change).
tldr.outcome: Shim6 enables site multihoming in IPv6 without PI prefix space, but requires careful consideration of address selection, traffic engineering, security, and interaction with other protocols like Mobile IPv6, SEND, and firewalls.

today: RFC 6629 is Informational and documents the applicability considerations for Shim6 as defined in RFC 5533 and RFC 5534. It guides operators in assessing whether Shim6 suits their multihoming needs.

sections.title: The Multihoming Problem in IPv6
sections.content: Site multihoming means connecting a network site to multiple Internet providers for better reliability. IPv4 solves this by injecting extra routing state (multiple routes for provider-independent prefixes) into the global Internet, but this approach does not scale to large numbers of sites. IPv6 offers a different path: the large address space lets hosts get one address from each provider and manage multiple addresses per interface. This avoids routing bloat but creates a new problem—when a path fails, transport-layer connections break because the addresses change. Shim6 solves this by inserting a thin layer (a shim) between the Internet layer and transport layer that makes address changes transparent to transport protocols, so connections survive re-homing events.
sections.eli5: You can get mail from two different post offices (two addresses), but phone calls break when you switch. Shim6 makes it so you can switch without the phone hanging up.

sections.title: The Multihomed Site Scenario
sections.content: The primary use case is a site connected to multiple transit providers (ISPs), each providing an IPv6 prefix. A host in that site receives one address from each provider's prefix. Shim6 runs on the host and monitors communications. When a connection is established, Shim6 creates a session and monitors for failures. If the currently active address pair fails—for example, if the inbound path through ISP[1] goes down—Shim6's failure detection mechanism tries alternative address combinations until it finds a working pair. Changing from address L[i] (routed through ISP[i]) to L[j] (routed through ISP[j]) effectively re-routes the inbound traffic through the alternate ISP. Outbound traffic routing depends on exit selection policies and address selection, which administrators must configure carefully to comply with ingress filtering and direct traffic to the correct provider.
sections.eli5: Your house has two mailboxes (two addresses), one for each road. If mail stops coming through one road, Shim6 switches the conversation to use the other mailbox.

sections.title: Address Handling and Security in Shim6
sections.content: Shim6 uses two types of addresses. Locators are the actual IP addresses used on the wire and change during re-homing. Upper-Layer Identifiers (ULIDs) are stable identifiers presented to the transport layer, so TCP ports and connections remain consistent. Security is based on Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA) or Hash-Based Addresses (HBA), which encode cryptographic information in the lower 64 bits of the address. This lets Shim6 verify that a claimed locator actually belongs to the peer, preventing address spoofing. CGAs require more computation but are more flexible; HBAs are faster. Stateless address auto-configuration (RFC 4862) can generate these addresses, but stateful configuration via DHCPv6 is not yet supported. IPv4 locators are not suitable because the address space is too small to include cryptographic data, and address translation (common in IPv4) breaks the verification.
sections.eli5: Your real name does not change (ULID), but your mailing addresses do (locators). Each address is sealed with a special signature so you can prove it is really yours.

sections.title: Fault Tolerance and Advanced Uses
sections.content: Shim6 provides fault tolerance for established connections: once a session is set up, failure detection finds a working locator pair if one exists and continues the communication transparently. However, Shim6 does not protect connection establishment—if a host picks a failed address to initiate a connection, the setup fails. It is most effective for long-lived flows, not short-lived transactions, because the 4-way handshake to establish a Shim6 session has overhead. Shim6 can also support host multihoming (multiple interfaces on one host) in addition to site multihoming, and could theoretically support load balancing and traffic engineering by choosing which locator pair to use, though load balancing is not the primary design goal.
sections.eli5: Once you are talking on the phone, Shim6 finds a working road if one exists. It works best for long phone calls, not quick text messages.

sections.title: Interactions with Other Protocols and Mechanisms
sections.content: Shim6 must coexist with many other IPv6 technologies. With Mobile IPv6, Shim6 can protect multihomed home networks and can run between a home agent and mobile node, but the details depend on the deployment model. SEND (Secure Neighbor Discovery) provides address-ownership verification; Shim6's CGA and HBA addresses are compatible. Shim6 interacts poorly with firewalls that track flows by address pairs, since Shim6 changes addresses mid-flow. NEMO (Network Mobility) extends Mobile IPv6 to mobile networks, and Shim6 can complement it. HIP (Host Identity Protocol) is an alternative multihoming approach with a different architecture. NPTv6 (network prefix translation) can interfere with Shim6's cryptographic addresses because translated addresses will not verify. SCTP and MPTCP (multipath transport protocols) offer alternative approaches to some of Shim6's goals at the transport layer.
sections.eli5: Shim6 has to play nicely with security protocols, mobile protocols, translation, and firewall rules. Some combinations work better than others.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Considerations
sections.content: The security model relies on cryptographically validated addresses (CGA/HBA) to ensure peers cannot be spoofed. Shim6 itself does not introduce new routing vulnerabilities because it operates on individual hosts, not in the DFZ. However, operators must carefully manage address selection policies to avoid ingress filtering problems (traffic filtered because it comes from an unexpected provider). Privacy considerations exist because Shim6 state is end-to-end; nodes exchange locators, which could leak information. The applicability of Shim6 depends on whether a site has multiple providers, whether operators want transport-layer stability across re-homing (or can tolerate connection breaks), and whether the administrative burden of address selection and traffic engineering policies is acceptable. For simple dual-provider scenarios with careful address configuration, Shim6 is applicable; for complex multihomed networks with advanced traffic engineering, additional mechanisms beyond Shim6 may be needed.
sections.eli5: Shim6 is secure against address spoofing but requires careful setup. It works best in simple multihomed sites, not complex networks.
